title: California's Big Gamble: Can a New Map Flip Congress?
summary: Picture a giant game of political chess. California just moved its pieces to try to win more seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. Why? Because Texas redrew its map to help Republicans, so California Democrats fought back. They got voters to let them draw new lines that could give them up to five extra seats. But there's a catch. In California's primary, the top two vote-getters move on, no matter their party. In a district near San Diego, a Republican seat was redrawn to lean slightly Democratic. The Republican congressman retired, so a local Republican supervisor, Jim Desmond, jumped in. But nine—yes, nine!—Democrats also want the job. If they split the vote too much, two Republicans could finish first and second, locking Democrats out of the November election entirely. "After millions of dollars and a nationwide effort to redraw these districts in response to Texas, Democrats being shut out would be a nightmare," said Ammar Campa-Najjar, one of the Democratic candidates. Other races are just as wild. In the Central Valley, a Republican who voted to impeach Trump faces two very different Democrats—one backed by the party establishment, one a progressive professor. And in San Francisco, the race to replace Nancy Pelosi has a tech entrepreneur who helped Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez win. Tuesday's primary will show if California's big gamble pays off—or backfires.
why_it_matters: Who gets elected to Congress can change laws about classroom technology, climate, and even how much homework you might have, so these primary results shape your future.

keywords.explanation: A primary is an election where voters choose which candidates will compete in the bigger, final election.
To impeach means to officially accuse a high official, like the president, of wrongdoing by the House of Representatives.
Progressive describes a person or idea that wants big social changes and more government action to help people.
In politics, the establishment is the group of people who have long been in power and control the party's direction.
Redraw means to draw new boundary lines, especially for voting districts, to change which voters live where.
Democrats are members of one of the two main U.S. political parties, often supporting a bigger role for government in solving problems.

background_read: California, the most populous U.S. state, has 52 seats in the House of Representatives, more than any other state, so its elections are closely watched.
Nancy Pelosi (the former Speaker of the House and a top Democrat) represented San Francisco for many years and is now leaving Congress, causing a rush to replace her.
Redistricting happens every ten years after the census, and sometimes parties redraw maps to give themselves an advantage—a practice called gerrymandering.
Article_Structure: WHO: California Democrats, Republican candidates like Jim Desmond, and Democratic candidates like Ammar Campa-Najjar
WHAT: California redrew its congressional maps to try to win more House seats, but the top-two primary system could accidentally lock Democrats out
WHERE: Multiple California districts, especially near San Diego, the Central Valley, and San Francisco
WHY: As a response to Texas redrawing its own map to help Republicans, Democrats want to flip enough seats to control Congress

perspectives.description: They see the map changes as a smart way to gain up to five seats and pass a Democratic agenda on climate, healthcare, and education.
They point out that splitting the Democratic vote could backfire, leaving no Democrat on the November ballot and reducing competition.
Many say redistricting is a normal power struggle between parties, but the top-two primary system adds an unpredictable twist rarely seen elsewhere.
